paragraphs: Needling for medical purposes predates any single date by centuries, and the practice grew out of even older techniques of bloodletting with sharpened stone or bone. What changed around this period was standardisation: physicians mapped named points along channels called meridians and matched them to specific ailments in written form.

The earliest surviving needles recovered from Han-era tombs are fine and made of metal, replacing the coarser bian stones of earlier centuries. The theory behind the points, that they regulate the flow of qi, has no equivalent in the anatomy Western medicine later described, which is why the two systems have never mapped cleanly onto each other.

Al-Razi ran a hospital in Baghdad and wrote several hundred works across medicine, philosophy and chemistry, only a fraction of which survive. His treatise on smallpox and measles set out symptoms of each side by side, from the character of the rash to the order in which fever and eruption appeared, so a physician could tell them apart before either ran its full course.

Latin translations carried the text into European medical schools for centuries after his death in 925. He also argued, unusually for his time, that a physician's reputation should rest on results rather than on reciting older authorities, and he was willing to say openly when Galen had got something wrong.

Al-Zahrawi worked as court physician in Cordoba and closed his medical encyclopedia, al-Tasrif, with a volume devoted entirely to surgery, illustrated with roughly two hundred instruments he designed or adapted himself. Many, including forceps for extracting a dead fetus and a hook still used for tonsillectomy, changed little for centuries after him.

He described cauterisation, the setting of fractures and dislocations, and the first known use of catgut for internal stitching, chosen because it dissolved on its own inside the body. Translated into Latin as the Liber Trotularis, no relation to the Salernitan Trotula, his surgical volume was taught in European universities into the sixteenth century.

Anatomy schools in Britain had run on a supply of stolen corpses, dug from fresh graves by body snatchers and sold to lecturers who needed cadavers to teach dissection. The murders committed by William Burke and William Hare in Edinburgh, who killed to sell bodies rather than digging them up, forced the issue into Parliament.

The Anatomy Act of 1832 gave licensed teachers legal access to unclaimed bodies from workhouses and hospitals instead, ending the grave-robbing trade almost overnight. It shifted the burden onto the poor, whose unclaimed dead now supplied dissection tables by default, a trade-off the law left largely unexamined for well over a century.

At Epidaurus, the largest of the god's sanctuaries, sick pilgrims slept overnight in a hall called the abaton, hoping Asclepius would visit them in a dream and prescribe a cure. Priests then interpreted the dream and administered whatever treatment it seemed to call for, from herbal draughts to a supervised regimen of diet and exercise.

Stone tablets recovered at the site record cures the sanctuary credited to the god, including surgery performed in sleep, claims no outsider verified. Non venomous snakes were kept loose in the temple precinct, since the animal was sacred to Asclepius and later became the symbol still attached to medicine.

Zidovudine, known as AZT, had already failed once. Jerome Horwitz synthesised it in 1964 as a possible cancer treatment, and it did not work well enough to matter. Two decades later, researchers screening old compounds against HIV found it blocked the virus's ability to copy its genetic material.

The FDA approved AZT in March 1987 after a trial stopped early because the drug's benefit looked too clear to keep placebo patients on nothing. It was not a cure, resistance developed quickly, and the high doses used at first caused severe side effects, but it was the first drug that gave AIDS patients any medical option at all.

Albert Calmette and Camille Guerin spent thirteen years weakening a strain of bovine tuberculosis bacteria by repeatedly culturing it on bile-soaked potato slices, hoping to breed a strain too feeble to cause disease but still able to provoke immunity. In 1921 they gave the resulting vaccine, BCG, to an infant in Paris whose mother had died of tuberculosis and whose grandmother had the disease.

Uptake was slow and a 1930 batch contaminated at Lubeck killed dozens of infants, feeding suspicion of the vaccine for years afterward. It nonetheless became the most widely given vaccine in history, part of routine childhood immunisation in most countries, even though its protection against adult lung tuberculosis remains inconsistent.

No single lab gets to claim the pill. Chemist Carl Djerassi's team in Mexico City synthesised a potent oral progestin from wild yams in 1951; biologist Gregory Pincus and gynaecologist John Rock then tested it on women, with funding from suffragist Katharine McCormick, who had wanted this exact project for years and finally paid for it herself.

Large trials ran in Puerto Rico from 1956, partly because contraceptive research faced legal restrictions in most American states at the time. The Food and Drug Administration approved the resulting drug, Enovid, as a contraceptive in May 1960, three years after this listed date, by which point it had already been prescribed widely for menstrual disorders under a more permissive label.

Bernard Fantus, director of therapeutics at Cook County Hospital, opened his blood preservation laboratory on 15 March 1937 to solve a specific problem: patients bleeding out while staff hunted for a donor with the right blood group. He coined the term blood bank himself, deliberately borrowing the language of deposits and withdrawals.

The lab cost about fifteen hundred dollars to set up and handled well over a thousand transfusions in its first year, using citrate to keep donated blood from clotting in storage. Cook County's model, with blood typed, stored and ready before it was needed, spread to other American hospitals within a few years and shaped blood banking through the Second World War.

Karl Landsteiner had shown by 1901 that mixing blood from different people often caused the red cells to clump, and sorted samples into what became groups A, B and O. For years this stayed a laboratory finding rather than a bedside habit, since most surgeons still transfused by guesswork or luck.

In 1907 the New York physician Reuben Ottenberg carried out what is considered the first transfusion actually matched by testing donor and recipient blood beforehand, and he also noted that group O blood caused fewer reactions in others. Routine cross-matching before transfusion followed from that practice rather than from Landsteiner's original discovery alone.

Celsus was not a practising physician but a wealthy Roman encyclopedist writing one section, De Medicina, of a much larger work covering agriculture, rhetoric and law that has otherwise been lost. His medical volume survived largely intact, making it the earliest substantial medical text in Latin rather than Greek.

He named heat, pain, redness and swelling as the four cardinal signs of inflammation, a list still taught under his Latin terms today. He also described cataract surgery, the removal of bladder stones, and amputation technique in enough procedural detail that later surgeons treated the text as a working manual, not just a summary.

James Simpson had promoted chloroform since 1847, but it was John Snow, not Simpson, who gave it to Queen Victoria on 7 April 1853 during the birth of Prince Leopold, dripping it onto a handkerchief over fifty-three minutes. Victoria called it that blessed chloroform and asked for it again four years later for Princess Beatrice.

Clergy and some doctors had argued pain in labour was biblically ordained, so a reigning monarch accepting anaesthesia carried weight the medical argument alone had not. British newspapers began calling the practice anesthesia a la reine, and objections to obstetric chloroform fell away faster after 1853 than before it.

Jesuit missionaries in Peru learned from local healers that the bitter bark of the cinchona tree eased fevers, and by the 1630s they were shipping ground bark back to Rome, where it became known as Jesuit's powder. It worked against malaria specifically, because the bark contains quinine, though nobody isolated that compound until 1820.

Protestant Europe was slow to trust a remedy tied to the Jesuit order, and Oliver Cromwell reportedly refused it on those grounds before dying of malarial fever in 1658. Cinchona bark remained the only real defence against the disease for roughly two centuries, until synthetic antimalarials replaced it in the twentieth century.

Constantine was born in North Africa and travelled through the Islamic world before settling at the monastery of Monte Cassino, where he translated Arabic medical texts, including works by al-Razi and Ibn al-Jazzar, into Latin. He rarely credited his sources, and some of what he presented as original was later shown to be close paraphrase of Arabic originals.

His translations reached the nearby medical school at Salerno, then the leading centre of medical teaching in Latin Christendom, and gave European physicians access to Greek medical theory that had been preserved and expanded in Arabic long after most of it was lost in the West. The practice of translating without attribution he set continued among later Latin translators for generations.

Godfrey Hounsfield built his scanner at EMI, the British record and electronics company better known for the Beatles, using its profits to fund research outside music entirely. On 1 October 1971 radiologist James Ambrose scanned a middle-aged woman suspected of having a brain tumour, and the machine found a cyst that ordinary X-rays could never have shown.

The physicist Alan Cormack had separately worked out the mathematics for reconstructing a cross-section from many X-ray readings back in the early 1960s, without knowing anyone would build the machine to use it. Hounsfield and Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, though Cormack had no part in EMI's actual scanner.

The antitoxin is usually dated to Emil von Behring alone, but he discovered it in 1890 jointly with the Japanese bacteriologist Shibasaburo Kitasato, injecting animals with diphtheria toxin and finding their blood serum could neutralise it in others. Paul Ehrlich then worked out how to standardise the serum's strength, without which dosing patients safely would have been guesswork.

Large-scale production began at Hoechst in 1894, and within a decade diphtheria death rates in treated children fell sharply across Europe. Behring alone received the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901, largely for this work; Kitasato's contribution to the original 1890 finding is now generally acknowledged but was not rewarded at the time.

Georg Ebers bought this scroll in Luxor in 1873, a century collectors spent buying up whatever the antiquities trade in that city could produce. Unrolled, it runs over twenty metres and mixes genuinely clinical description with incantations against demons blamed for disease, medicine and magic on the same page with no line drawn between them.

Among roughly 700 remedies is an early description of tumours and instructions for treating them, alongside a passage often read as the first written reference to diabetes, an ailment marked by frequent urination. Most prescriptions rely on plants, minerals and animal fat rather than the spells that surround them.

Edwin Smith bought the papyrus in Luxor in 1862. It sat untranslated for decades until James Henry Breasted published it in 1930, revealing forty-eight case studies of injuries running from the skull down to the spine, each set out as examination, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis.

The copy dates to around 1600 BCE, but its content is older still and echoes battlefield surgery rather than magic. It offers the earliest known description of the brain's surface and the first note that head wounds could paralyse the opposite side of the body, a link no other ancient text draws.

Paul Ehrlich screened hundreds of numbered arsenic compounds against syphilis before settling on the 606th, which his laboratory patented in 1910 as Salvarsan. He had spent years chasing a substance that would kill an infecting organism while leaving the patient's own cells alone, a goal he described as a magic bullet.

Salvarsan had to be injected in large, painful doses and carried real risks of its own, but it was the first drug designed from a specific chemical target rather than found by trial in nature. It gave the young field its name, chemotherapy, meaning treatment by chemical compound, well before the word narrowed to cancer drugs.

Padua's university had been holding public dissections for over a century before this permanent theatre was built in 1594, but earlier ones used temporary wooden stands assembled and taken down each winter. The new structure, designed under anatomist Girolamo Fabrici, packed rings of standing spectators steeply around a small central table, since dissection had to finish before a body without preservation began to decay.

Students from across Europe travelled to Padua specifically to study there, including William Harvey, who later described the circulation of the blood. The theatre still stands within the university today, one of the oldest surviving purpose-built teaching spaces in medicine.

Stephen Hales, an English clergyman and scientist, tied a mare down in 1733 and inserted a brass tube connected to a goose windpipe into an artery in her neck. Blood surged up a vertical glass tube attached to it and settled more than eight feet above the level of her heart, rising and falling slightly with each pulse.

It was the first direct measurement of blood pressure ever recorded, and Hales went on to show it varied with body size, exercise and the stage of the heartbeat. His method was invasive and fatal to the animal, and doctors would not have a way to measure blood pressure in a living, uninjured person until the sphygmomanometer arrived more than a century later.

Jesse Bennett is said to have operated on his own wife Elizabeth in their Virginia cabin on 14 January 1794, after a fellow physician who had been called in refused to attempt the delivery and declared her likely to die. Bennett cut into her himself, delivered the child, and by most accounts she recovered within weeks.

The story rests on family retellings rather than a contemporary medical record, and historians disagree even about whether Bennett had formal medical training. What is not disputed is that a maternal cesarean survival in America this early was exceptional: without antisepsis or reliable anaesthesia, the operation usually killed the mother, and Elizabeth Bennett is reported to have lived for decades afterward.

James Lind was a naval surgeon aboard HMS Salisbury when he split twelve scurvy-stricken sailors into six pairs in 1747, giving each pair a different treatment: cider, vinegar, seawater, a spiced paste, sulphuric acid, or two oranges and a lemon. All the men otherwise ate the same rations and shared quarters, which is what makes the setup a genuine controlled comparison rather than an anecdote.

The citrus pair recovered fastest, one man well enough to nurse the others within days. Lind published the result in 1753 but buried it in a long treatise still weighted toward older humoral theory, and the Royal Navy did not issue lemon juice as standard until 1795, four decades after his trial.

John Greenwood, one of George Washington's dentists, adapted his mother's spinning wheel around 1790, rigging its foot pedal to spin a drill bit instead of thread. Before it, dentists rotated drills by hand or by twisting a cord between finger and thumb, which limited both speed and how long a treatment could last.

The foot-powered wheel freed his hands to hold the instrument steady while his foot kept it turning, cutting decayed tooth material faster and more evenly than a hand drill could manage. Later nineteenth-century dentists refined the same pedal principle into geared treadle drills, before electric motors replaced foot power entirely in the twentieth century.

Isabelle Dinoire had been mauled by her dog while unconscious, losing her nose, lips and chin. In November 2005, surgeons Bernard Devauchelle and Jean-Michel Dubernard in Amiens grafted a triangle of nose, lips and chin taken from a brain-dead donor onto her face, the first partial transplant of its kind.

The operation raised questions medicine had not faced before: a face carries identity in a way a kidney does not, and Dinoire had to adjust to seeing a hybrid of her own features and a stranger's. She lived with the transplant for eleven years on immunosuppressant drugs, and later, more extensive full-face transplants followed her case directly.

On 30 August 2017 the FDA approved tisagenlecleucel, sold as Kymriah, for children and young adults with a form of leukaemia that had relapsed after other treatment. The therapy takes a patient's own immune cells, genetically edits them to hunt cells carrying a marker called CD19, and infuses them back in.

In the trial that supported approval, most of the 63 young patients treated went into remission within three months, a result striking enough to earn breakthrough designation. The approach, developed at the University of Pennsylvania and licensed to Novartis, opened a new category of cancer treatment built from a patient's own reprogrammed cells rather than a manufactured drug.

The vaccine approved in the United States in 1981, developed largely under Maurice Hilleman at Merck, was made from purified surface-antigen particles taken from the blood plasma of chronic hepatitis B carriers. It was an unusual source for a vaccine, and it worked, though a recombinant version made in yeast soon replaced it.

Hepatitis B causes chronic liver infection that can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer over decades, so the vaccine's real effect showed up only slowly. Taiwan's mass infant vaccination programme, started in 1984, was later linked to a measurable fall in childhood liver cancer, among the first vaccines shown to prevent a cancer directly.

John Charnley, an English orthopaedic surgeon, had already tried and abandoned a Teflon hip joint that wore out fast inside the body before settling in 1962 on a design pairing a metal stem with a high-density polyethylene socket, cemented into the bone with acrylic. He worked mostly at a small hospital in Wrightington, testing components on himself as much as on patients.

The low-friction combination of metal and plastic, lubricated by the body's own joint fluid, proved durable enough to last years rather than months. Variations on Charnley's basic design, metal ball against plastic socket, still make up most hip replacements performed today, an operation now done well over a million times a year worldwide.

Basil, bishop of Caesarea, built his complex during and after the famine of 369, when he had already emptied his own inheritance feeding the starving. Known as the Basiliad, it grew to include a hospice, an orphanage, workshops, and housing for physicians and nursing staff who worked there for pay rather than as an act of charity alone.

A ward set aside for people with leprosy was its most striking feature. Basil reportedly visited and embraced patients others would not touch, and offered training meant to let recovered residents return to ordinary life. Later Byzantine and medieval European hospitals borrowed the same combination of medical care, shelter and religious oversight under one roof.

Steven Trokel had already shown that an excimer laser could etch human corneal tissue with startling precision, vaporising thin layers without damaging what lay beneath. In 1987, working from that research, surgeons in the United States and West Germany began using the laser on patients to reshape the cornea's curvature, though sources disagree on exactly who performed the very first case.

The technique, photorefractive keratectomy, treated the cornea's surface directly rather than cutting a flap into it, and became the basis for the flap-based LASIK procedures that followed in the 1990s. Together they turned a laser built for industrial precision work into a routine outpatient treatment for short-sightedness.

Thomas Starzl's actual first attempt, in March 1963 in Denver, ended on the operating table when the recipient bled to death; the child had haemophilia, a complication no one had anticipated. His second attempt that May, on a 48-year-old man named William Grisby, succeeded as surgery, but Grisby died weeks later of complications while the transplanted liver itself was still functioning.

Starzl and a French team both tried liver transplants in humans in 1963, and none of the first several patients anywhere lived beyond a year. The obstacle was rejection, not surgical technique: only with the drug ciclosporin in the early 1980s did Starzl achieve transplants his patients actually survived long-term.

James Hardy transplanted a lung into John Russell, a dying convict, at the University of Mississippi on 11 June 1963, using a donor organ from a man who had just died of a heart attack. Russell had lung cancer and had agreed to the untested operation as a last option.

The lung itself worked reasonably well, but Russell died eighteen days later of kidney failure and malnutrition unrelated to the transplant. It was still the first human lung transplant on record, and the fifteen years of failures that followed it, mostly from rejection and leaking airway connections, were not solved until Joel Cooper's first long-term survivor in 1983.

Malaria vaccines had been tried for decades and mostly failed, because the parasite changes shape across its life cycle and outruns simple immunity. Mosquirix, known as RTS,S, targets one stage of that cycle, and after pilot programmes vaccinated over 800,000 children in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi, the WHO recommended it for wide use in October 2021.

It is only partially effective, cutting severe cases by roughly thirty per cent rather than preventing infection outright, and needs several doses. Even so, it was the first vaccine ever approved against any parasitic disease in humans, aimed at an illness that still kills several hundred thousand children under five each year.

The British Lying-In Hospital opened in London in 1749, following the smaller Middlesex Hospital's maternity ward established in 1745, and a cluster of similar charitable lying-in hospitals followed within a few years. They were built for poor married women who could not afford a private midwife or physician and had nowhere safe to give birth.

Conditions inside were mixed: the hospitals cut maternal deaths from starvation and exposure but crowded new mothers together in ways that let puerperal fever spread between wards, sometimes killing more women than home birth would have. It took another century, and Ignaz Semmelweis's handwashing studies in the 1840s, before hospitals understood why.

Frederick II issued his medical statutes as part of the Constitutions of Melfi, a broader law code covering the Kingdom of Sicily. The rules required anyone practising medicine to pass an examination set by masters at Salerno and to obtain a licence from the crown, on pain of fines and confiscation of property for practising without one.

The statutes also separated the roles of physician and apothecary, forbidding a doctor from owning a share in a pharmacy, to stop physicians profiting by prescribing expensive remedies. Salerno's medical school, already established for two centuries, became the examining body the law leaned on, tying royal authority to an existing academic institution rather than creating a new one.

Benjamin Franklin Palmer lost his own leg below the knee as a boy in Meredith, New Hampshire, and grew up dissatisfied with the rigid pegs available to amputees. In 1846 he patented an artificial leg with an ankle joint that flexed as the wearer walked, rather than forcing a stiff, swinging gait.

Palmer's design won praise at London's Great Exhibition of 1851 and sold well enough that he opened workshops on both sides of the Atlantic. The American Civil War, a few years later, created tens of thousands of amputees and turned articulated prosthetics from a novelty into an industry with sustained demand.

Florence Nightingale wrote Notes on Nursing from her sickbed, having been left an invalid by the Crimean War, and never worked as a hospital nurse in Britain again. It was aimed at ordinary women running a household, not trained staff, opening with the line that every woman is at some point a nurse.

The book insisted that cleanliness, fresh air, quiet and light mattered more than medicine, drawing on the sanitary statistics she had gathered at Scutari. It sold cheaply and widely, and its 1860 popular edition helped fix nursing as a discipline with its own rules rather than an extension of housework.

Anthony Atala's team at Wake Forest took a small biopsy of bladder tissue from each patient, grew the muscle and lining cells separately in culture, and seeded them onto a biodegradable scaffold shaped like a bladder. The scaffold dissolved over time, leaving an organ built almost entirely from the patient's own cells.

The surgeries had actually been carried out years earlier, on children with spina bifida whose bladders did not function properly, but the results were only published in the Lancet in 2006, which is when the achievement became public. Because the tissue was the patient's own, there was no rejection risk, an advantage organ transplants from donors can never offer.

The Dispensatorium was written by Valerius Cordus, a botanist who died in Rome in 1544 at twenty-nine and never saw it printed. Nuremberg published it in 1546 and, unusually for the time, made it the compulsory standard every apothecary in the city had to follow rather than a reference they could ignore.

Before it, druggists mixed remedies from a jumble of regional recipe books with no shared measures or ingredients. Cordus's list fixed exact formulas and doses, and other German and Dutch cities adopted it wholesale or copied its structure, making it the model other places pointed to when they wrote pharmacopoeias of their own.

David Bennett Sr. had heart failure too advanced to qualify for a human transplant list. In January 2022, surgeon Bartley Griffith and his team at the University of Maryland gave him a heart from a pig genetically edited by the biotech company Revivicor, with genes removed that would have triggered immediate rejection by a human immune system.

Bennett lived for two months afterward before dying, and investigators later found signs of a pig virus that may have contributed. The operation was still treated as a genuine step forward for xenotransplantation, a field trying to close the enormous gap between the number of people needing organs and the number of human donors available.

Louis Pasteur had only tested his rabies treatment on dogs when a nine-year-old boy, Joseph Meister, was brought to him in July 1885 after being severely bitten by a rabid dog. Rabies was, at the time, a certain and agonising death once symptoms began, so Pasteur's untested vaccine was the only option left.

Over thirteen days he gave Meister a series of injections made from dried, weakened rabbit spinal cord infected with the virus. The boy never developed rabies. Pasteur, who was a chemist rather than a physician and had no licence to treat patients, had gambled on a treatment that worked and effectively founded modern immunotherapy.

John Graunt was a London haberdasher, not a physician, when he began combing through the city's weekly Bills of Mortality in the 1650s. His 1662 book Natural and Political Observations turned decades of parish burial records into tables showing how many people died of what, at what age and in which season.

He estimated London's population from burial counts, noticed that roughly the same proportion of boys and girls were born each year, and showed plague deaths spiking in ways the raw bills alone never made visible. The Royal Society elected him a fellow on the strength of it, and his tables gave later epidemiologists their first working model for counting disease across a whole population.

Akira Endo was not looking for a heart drug. Working at the Japanese pharmaceutical company Sankyo, he screened thousands of fungi for compounds that might block cholesterol synthesis, reasoning that a mould defending itself against competing microbes might make one. In 1976 he isolated compactin from Penicillium citrinum.

Compactin itself never reached the market, but it proved a class of drugs worked, and Endo's approach led directly to lovastatin and the statins that followed. Decades of trials later, statins became among the most widely prescribed medicines in the world, credited with lowering heart attack and stroke rates across whole populations.

Almroth Wright developed a killed-bacteria vaccine against typhoid in 1896 while working at the Army Medical School in Netley, testing it first on himself and on soldiers bound for India. It was one of the earliest attempts to protect against a bacterial disease by injecting dead bacteria rather than a live weakened strain.

The British Army made the vaccine available but not compulsory in the Boer War, and typhoid killed far more soldiers there than combat did, a failure Wright blamed on low uptake. By the First World War inoculation was effectively routine for British troops, and typhoid deaths among them fell to a fraction of earlier wars.

Ian Donald, a Glasgow obstetrician who had used sonar to hunt submarines during the war, teamed up with engineer Tom Brown and obstetrician John MacVicar to point industrial ultrasound equipment, borrowed from a Clydeside boilermaker, at pregnant patients instead of steel plates.

Their 1958 paper in The Lancet showed scans distinguishing ovarian cysts from fibroids and identifying twins and fetal position, all without a single X-ray. Because it used sound rather than radiation, the technique could be repeated safely throughout a pregnancy, and it became routine antenatal care within Donald's own lifetime.

Girolamo Fracastoro published De Contagione in 1546, more than three centuries before anyone could see a microbe. He proposed disease passed between people through seminaria, invisible seed-like particles, and distinguished three routes of spread: direct touch, contaminated objects such as clothing, and transmission across distance through the air.

The book had no microscope to back it and made little difference to how physicians actually treated patients at the time, since bleeding and purging carried on regardless. It is remembered now mainly because germ theory, established properly in the 1860s and 1870s, ended up describing something close to what Fracastoro had guessed at without any evidence he could point to.

Guy de Chauliac was physician to three popes at Avignon and lived through the Black Death there in 1348, an outbreak he described firsthand and caught himself while continuing to treat the sick. His account of the plague's two forms, one striking the lungs and killing within days, remains one of the fullest surviving clinical descriptions of that outbreak.

His treatise, the Chirurgia Magna, drew on Arabic surgeons including al-Zahrawi and covered fractures, hernia repair and cataract surgery in careful procedural detail. It stayed the standard surgical reference across much of Europe for roughly two centuries, still being printed and consulted well after Chauliac's own death in 1368.

Herophilus worked in Alexandria under royal patronage from the Ptolemies, who had no religious objection to opening a corpse, unlike most of the ancient Mediterranean. He traced nerves from the brain rather than the heart, distinguished arteries from veins by their pulse, and named the retina and the duodenum.

Later writers, chiefly Celsus and Galen, accused him of vivisecting condemned criminals handed over by the king, cutting into living bodies rather than dead ones. No account from Herophilus's own time makes that claim, and the number given, in the hundreds, is now widely treated as later exaggeration rather than record.

The oath was not written by Hippocrates himself, and scholars are not certain who composed it or exactly when within his lifetime and the century after his death. It survives as part of a much larger body of writing, the Hippocratic Corpus, gathered from several authors and later attributed wholesale to one physician.

The original text swears by Apollo and several other gods, bans surgery for bladder stones as a specialist's job, and forbids giving a deadly drug even if asked for one. Modern medical schools that administer an oath at graduation almost always use a rewritten version, not this one.

Samuel Hahnemann, a German physician, dosed himself with cinchona bark in the 1790s and noticed it gave him fever-like symptoms similar to malaria itself. From that he built the principle of like cures like, treating illness with a substance that produces similar symptoms in a healthy person, diluted repeatedly until, by his own arithmetic, almost none of the original substance remained.

He published the system in 1796 partly as a reaction against contemporary medicine's harsher standard treatments of bleeding, purging and mercury, which often did more harm than the disease. Modern chemistry finds no mechanism by which dilutions that extreme could have any pharmacological effect, but homeopathy still has practitioners and regulated products in several countries today.

Gardasil, approved by the FDA in June 2006, grew out of virus-like particle work by Ian Frazer and the late Jian Zhou at the University of Queensland, who found that a single viral protein could self-assemble into an empty shell resembling the real virus closely enough to trigger immunity.

Because cervical cancer is caused almost entirely by a handful of HPV strains, a vaccine against the virus itself, rather than the cancer, was a genuinely new strategy against a cancer. Uptake varied hugely by country, and Australia, an early and aggressive adopter, later reported cervical cancer rates falling toward levels low enough to call the disease rare.

Hua Tuo practised during the collapse of the Han dynasty and treated the warlord Cao Cao for severe headaches, according to the Book of Later Han and the Records of the Three Kingdoms. When Hua Tuo proposed cutting into Cao Cao's skull, the warlord suspected an assassination attempt, imprisoned him, and had him executed. Hua Tuo's medical writings were said to have been burned with him.

His anaesthetic, mafeisan, combined wine with an herbal powder whose exact recipe was lost with his texts. Historians cannot confirm from the surviving descriptions whether it produced full surgical unconsciousness or only heavy sedation, and no independent contemporary source corroborates the abdominal operations later legend credits to him.

The Yellow Emperor whose name the text carries did not write it and, if he existed at all, lived over two thousand years before it was assembled. The book is a dialogue between him and his physician Qi Bo, a literary device that let later compilers fold centuries of accumulated theory into one voice.

It sets out the body as a balance of yin and yang and a flow of qi through channels, the framework acupuncture still names its points against today. Two surviving sections, one on theory and one on needling technique, were pieced together from fragments over the following centuries rather than handed down whole.

A draft covering most of the genome had already been announced in 2000 with considerable fanfare. The Human Genome Project declared its sequence essentially finished in April 2003, timed to the fiftieth anniversary of Watson and Crick's DNA structure paper, after a public consortium and a private competitor, Celera Genomics, had raced each other through the 1990s.

Even the finished version left small gaps and repetitive regions unresolved for years afterward; a fully gapless sequence was not produced until 2022. What the 2003 milestone delivered was a working reference genome, letting researchers locate disease genes by comparing a patient's DNA against a known map rather than searching blind.

Shinya Yamanaka's team at Kyoto University tested twenty-four candidate genes thought to keep embryonic stem cells flexible, then narrowed them down one at a time. In 2006 they found that inserting just four, now called the Yamanaka factors, into an adult mouse skin cell could reset it to an embryonic-like state.

The result meant an adult cell could become almost any tissue type without using an embryo at all, sidestepping the ethical fights that had surrounded stem cell research for years. Human cells were reprogrammed the same way within a year. Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize with John Gurdon, whose 1962 cloning work had shown cell identity could be reversed.

Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw, working at Harvard, built their respirator in 1928 as a sealed metal tank that enclosed a patient's body up to the neck, using bellows to cycle air pressure inside and force the chest to rise and fall. It was meant for anyone whose breathing muscles had failed, not polio specifically, and their first working model was tested on a cat.

Polio made the machine famous. When paralysis reached the muscles that drive breathing, a patient could survive for weeks or years inside one, and photographs of hospital wards lined with iron lungs became a defining image of the epidemics of the 1940s and 1950s. Engineer John Emerson's cheaper version from 1931 was what most hospitals actually bought.

Gallbladder removal had always meant a long incision across the abdomen and a recovery measured in weeks. In March 1987, in Lyon, the French surgeon Philippe Mouret removed a patient's gallbladder using instruments passed through a handful of small punctures, guided by a camera rather than a direct view into the open abdomen.

Mouret had not set out to revolutionise surgery, having combined a gynaecological laparoscopy with a gallbladder case almost incidentally, but the technique spread within a few years to become the default approach for that operation worldwide. Patients went home in days instead of weeks, and laparoscopic methods were soon adapted to a wide range of other procedures.

Ali Maow Maalin worked as a hospital cook in Merca, Somalia, and had refused smallpox vaccination out of fear of the needle. In October 1977 he caught the disease anyway, becoming the last person on record to acquire it through ordinary transmission rather than a laboratory accident. He survived.

His case triggered an intense containment effort: health workers vaccinated everyone he had contact with, and no further chain of natural infection was ever traced. The World Health Organisation certified smallpox eradicated in 1980. Maalin later worked as a polio vaccinator, helping fight the disease he had once refused protection against.

By the twelfth century, European towns were building leprosaria on their outskirts by the thousand, often just beyond the walls where residents could receive alms from travellers passing on the road. Some estimates put the total across medieval Europe near nineteen thousand, though record keeping was too uneven for that figure to be treated as exact.

Admission usually followed a formal rite resembling a funeral mass, since the afflicted were treated as dead to ordinary society even while still living within the leprosarium's own community. Diagnosis rested on visible signs alone, so the institutions almost certainly held people with other skin diseases alongside those who genuinely had leprosy.

By 1871 Joseph Lister was pumping a fine carbolic acid mist over the operating table from a device nicknamed the donkey engine, meant to kill germs floating in the air before they reached an open wound. It followed his earlier practice of soaking dressings and instruments in the same acid, first tried on a compound fracture in Glasgow in 1865.

The spray stung surgeons eyes and lungs for two decades before Lister gave it up. By 1887 he had concluded that airborne germs mattered far less than those carried on hands, instruments and dressings, and in 1890 he told a Berlin audience he was ashamed of having recommended it. The hand-washing and clean-instrument habits it left behind outlasted the machine itself.

Mondino de Luzzi taught at Bologna, where he dissected at least two female bodies himself rather than relying only on animal anatomy or ancient texts, an approach most European medicine had abandoned for over a millennium. His manual, the Anathomia, organised the body by the order a dissector would actually cut through it, starting with the abdomen because it decayed fastest.

The text leaned heavily on Galen and Avicenna and repeated some of their errors uncorrected, since Mondino trusted the old authorities even where his own knife showed something different. Even so, it became the standard European teaching text for public dissections for the next two centuries, including at Padua's later anatomy theatre.

Cesar Milstein and Georges Kohler worked in Cambridge on a problem that had nothing to do with diagnostics: how antibody diversity is generated. In 1975 they fused a mouse myeloma cell with an antibody-producing spleen cell, making a hybrid that divided endlessly while still churning out one identical antibody.

That hybridoma technique gave medicine a reliable factory for antibodies of known specificity, something no immune system offers on demand. It underpins pregnancy tests, cancer therapies and much of modern diagnostics. Milstein and Kohler never patented the method, sharing the 1984 Nobel Prize with Niels Jerne instead.

Giovanni Morgagni was in his late seventies in 1761 when he published De Sedibus et Causis Morborum, drawing on roughly seven hundred autopsies he had performed or reviewed across a long career in Padua. For each case he matched the symptoms a patient had described in life against the specific organ damage he found afterward on the table.

That pairing sounds obvious now, but medicine before him mostly located disease in the body's fluids as a whole rather than in one organ. By tying a cough to a diseased lung or dropsy to a failing heart, Morgagni gave doctors a reason to look for a physical seat of illness, which is the basic assumption modern pathology still starts from.

Hermann von Helmholtz built the ophthalmoscope in 1850 to answer a question from his own physiology students, why a pupil sometimes looks black and sometimes glows. His answer was a simple arrangement of angled glass plates and a light source that let him bounce light into someone's eye and see the illuminated retina reflected back through the same aperture.

He was not the first to notice the effect: Jan Purkinje had described it decades earlier and Charles Babbage built a similar device around 1847, but neither publicised the work. Helmholtz's version, published in 1851, was practical and well described enough that ophthalmologists adopted it quickly, and for the first time could examine a living retina for detached tissue or disease without surgery.

George Papanicolaou published his cervical smear method with gynaecologist Herbert Traut in 1943, having spent over a decade studying vaginal cell samples from women at New York Hospital. A year earlier, in 1927, the Romanian physician Aurel Babes had described a broadly similar method for detecting cervical cancer in a French journal, using a different sampling and staining technique.

Papanicolaou's version, with its own fixation and staining protocol, was the one adopted into routine screening, and English-language medicine named the test after him alone; Romania still calls it the Babes-Papanicolaou method. Wherever the credit lands, mass screening with it cut cervical cancer deaths substantially over the following decades by catching disease before symptoms appeared.

Paracelsus burned the standard textbooks of Galen and Avicenna in Basel in 1527, telling students their authors knew less than his own shoe buckles. He treated illness as a chemical imbalance to be corrected with mercury, antimony and sulphur rather than the four humours doctors had balanced with bleeding and purging for over a thousand years.

He also coined the toxicology principle that the dose makes the poison, arguing that any substance could heal or kill depending on quantity. Contemporaries mostly saw an abrasive outsider who lost his university post within two years, and it took later generations of iatrochemists to turn his mineral remedies into a lasting branch of medicine.

Ambroise Pare ran out of boiling oil during a siege in Turin in 1537 and dressed the remaining wounded with a soothing mixture of egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine instead. He expected them to fare worse overnight and found the opposite: the cauterised men were in agony while the others slept and healed.

He wrote up the finding and later replaced cautery for amputations with ligature, tying off blood vessels with thread rather than searing them shut. Pare had no formal Latin medical training and worked his way up as an army barber-surgeon, which made his 1545 published account harder for the university-trained physicians of Paris to dismiss.

Philippe Pinel took charge of the Bicetre asylum in Paris in 1793, during the Revolution's Terror, and ordered chains removed from patients who had been shackled for years. The often-told image of Pinel personally striking the irons off is a later embellishment; the actual unchaining at Bicetre was carried out mainly by an asylum attendant, Jean-Baptiste Pussin, whose methods Pinel adopted and then publicised.

Pinel replaced restraint and punishment with what he called moral treatment: routine, useful work, and observation instead of the whip. He moved to the Salpetriere hospital in 1795 and applied the same approach there, and his case records became an early argument that mental illness could be studied and treated rather than simply locked away.

Santorio Santorio built a chair suspended from a large steelyard balance and ate, worked and slept in it for roughly thirty years starting around 1614, weighing himself and everything he consumed and excreted. He found that his body lost weight overnight that food and waste alone could not account for, and called the missing mass insensible perspiration.

The chair itself, described in his book De Statica Medicina, made him one of the first people to apply a measuring instrument to the living body rather than to a corpse or a substance in a flask. His numbers were rough and his theory of humours was still Galenic, but the habit of weighing rather than guessing carried through into later physiology.

Lady Mary Wortley Montagu watched Ottoman women in Istanbul scratch smallpox matter from a mild case into a healthy person's skin, a practice that gave a controlled, usually survivable infection instead of the disease caught by chance. She had her own son inoculated there in 1718 and pushed the method in London after returning, having survived smallpox herself and lost her looks and a brother to it.

In 1721 English doctors tested variolation on condemned prisoners at Newgate, who were offered a pardon in exchange, before it spread among the aristocracy. It carried a real risk of death and of starting new outbreaks, and safer vaccination using cowpox, developed by Edward Jenner in 1796, eventually replaced it.

The description credits Selman Waksman's team, but streptomycin was isolated in 1943 by his graduate student Albert Schatz, working alone in a Rutgers basement lab on soil bacteria while Waksman was largely absent. Schatz was named first author on the discovery papers and co-held the original patent.

Two years later Waksman pressured Schatz into signing away his royalty share, without disclosing that Waksman himself was quietly taking twenty percent of the drug's earnings from Rutgers. Schatz sued once he found out and won a settlement along with formal recognition as co-discoverer, but Waksman alone kept the 1952 Nobel Prize for a drug that made tuberculosis, until then often a death sentence, curable.

What circulated as one text by one author, Trotula, is actually three separate treatises on women's conditions, treatments and cosmetics, probably written by different people. Only the middle one, on treatments, can be tied with any confidence to a real Salernitan practitioner named Trota, who taught and treated patients in the twelfth century.

Because Trota's name was the only one attached to any of the three works, later copyists credited her with the whole compiled set, and the title Trotula was eventually read as a person's name rather than as little Trota's book. The texts covered menstruation, childbirth and infertility with a directness rare in medieval medical writing aimed largely at male readers.

Casimir Funk was working in London in 1912 on beriberi, a disease common among people eating polished rice, when he isolated a nitrogen-containing compound from rice husks that cured it in pigeons. He guessed, wrongly as it turned out, that all such essential nutrients would share that amine chemistry, and coined vitamine from vital and amine.

The final e was dropped once other vitamins were shown not to be amines at all, giving the modern word vitamin. Funk's real insight survived the correction: several unrelated diseases, including beriberi, scurvy and rickets, were caused not by a germ but by the simple absence of a specific substance in the diet.

Richard Wiseman treated gunshot wounds on both sides of England's civil wars before serving as surgeon to Charles II, and his 1676 book Severall Chirurgicall Treatises drew on that battlefield casework rather than classroom theory. He described gangrene, aneurysm and gunshot injury from direct observation at a time when most English surgical writing still leaned on translated continental texts.

Later historians gave him the title father of English surgery, though the label reflects English medicine's own account of its history more than any settled international judgement, since French and Italian surgeons of the same period made comparable claims for themselves. Wiseman's case notes were still cited by British surgeons a century after his death in 1676.

William Withering learned of foxglove as a folk cure from a Shropshire herbalist known locally as the wise woman, who used it in a family recipe for dropsy, the swelling now recognised as heart failure. He spent about a decade testing doses on his own patients before publishing An Account of the Foxglove in 1785.

His book set out exact dried-leaf doses and warned how easily the plant could poison rather than cure, since the gap between an effective amount and a fatal one is narrow. Digoxin, the purified derivative still prescribed for heart failure and irregular rhythms today, traces directly back to Withering's careful dosing rather than to any single discovery moment.
